Workspace

SVGCraft edits on tablets and larger screens. A phone (narrower than 768 px, or a phone held sideways) gets a preview instead: open SVGs, switch between tabs, pan and pinch-zoom, Fit, and Info. The editing tools, menus and panels are hidden, and nothing on a phone changes a drawing. On tablets in portrait, the toolbar moves to the bottom and the panels slide in from the right (the sliders button).

The phone toolbar also has:

  • ▶ Play the drawing's animations (■ or a tap on it stops them; greyed out when nothing is animated).
  • Layers: the layer list, each with a preview (always on the checkerboard, as in the Layers panel) and an eye, to show and hide layers while you look. Only the preview changes: nothing is saved, and switching tab or moving to a bigger screen shows the drawing as it is again. Hide all / Show all do every layer (Show all includes ones the file itself hides); layers inside a hidden group are dimmed.
  • Text view (</>): the SVG source full-screen, syntax-coloured, to read (long lines wrapped), search and Copy (or download); the same button (now a picture) goes back to the drawing.
  • Background: the artwork on the checkerboard, white or black; each tap moves to the next, and the button shows which it's on (a checkered circle, white ringed in black, or black ringed in white). Remembered.
  • Share: the phone's share sheet with the SVG and a PNG of it (downloads the SVG where the browser can't share files).
  • Info (ⓘ): the drawing's details (file, size, dimensions, layers, animations, fonts) and its metadata from File Info (title, author, description, keywords, date, copyright, licence and source, linked), read-only, with About SVGCraft at the bottom.

Double-tap the canvas to zoom in on that spot (to 100%, or twice the fit for small drawings), and again to fit. Swipe along the tab bar for the next or previous drawing (while all the tabs fit).

Offline, and as an app. Once SVGCraft has been opened from the web, it works offline: a service worker keeps its files. Browsers that can install web apps offer to install it (Chrome and Edge: the install icon in the address bar, or File → Install SVGCraft…; iPhone and iPad: Share → Add to Home Screen). Installed, it opens in a window of its own, and on desktop Chrome and Edge it can be chosen to open .svg files. Opened straight from disk (file://), none of this applies.

The layout follows Photoshop:

  • Menu bar: File, Edit, Image, Layer, Object, Type, Select, View, Window and Help menus, in Photoshop's order. Layer holds what works on whole layers (New, Duplicate, Layer Style, Clipping Mask, Group, Arrange, Align, Lock); Object holds symbols and what works on shapes (Path, Combine Shapes, Flip). Click to open, hover to switch between them, and use the arrow keys to move around. As in Photoshop, an item or button that can't run on the current selection is greyed out: Crop to Selection needs a selection, a clipping mask, Combine Shapes or Text on Path need two layers, Distribute three, and so on. Its tooltip still shows, and its shortcut does nothing until it can run.
  • Options bar: settings for the current tool, such as stroke width and smoothing for the pencil, mode and size for the eraser, or the point commands for Edit Points. Drag a field's label sideways to scrub its value (Shift scrubs 10× faster).
  • Toolbar: the tools, with the fill and stroke chips at the bottom. Click a chip to make it the active paint, and click it again to pick a colour. Below the chips are swap (X) and "none".
  • Pointers are Photoshop's: the Move tool's arrow and cross, Edit Points' white arrow, a cross or lasso for picking points (with + while Shift adds, − while Alt takes away), the pen's nib (* to start a path, o over its first point to close it), the pencil, the eyedropper, the type I-beam and the curved arrow on the rotate handle.
  • Document tabs above the canvas, one per open drawing, showing the file name and zoom (see Documents below).
  • Panel heights, as in Photoshop: each group keeps its height whatever its tab shows (longer content scrolls inside it), so selecting something never shuffles the panels below. Drag the divider under a group to resize it (double-click it for the group's natural height, or use the arrow keys); Layers takes the rest and always keeps room. Remembered; Reset Workspace puts them back.
  • Docked panels: Color (fill and stroke, with the stroke's width, alignment, caps, joins and dashes) / Swatches / Gradients / Patterns, Properties (shape settings, document size, grid and snap), Character / Paragraph, Symbols, Animation and Layers (see below). As in Photoshop, each tab is an icon; the open tab also shows its name, and hovering any tab names it. Double-click a group's tab bar, or click the chevron at its end, to fold it to just its tabs (Layers then gets the room); clicking a tab opens it again. Folded groups stay folded on your next visit. The » button above the panels shrinks the whole column to a strip of their icons, leaving more room for the canvas; an icon pops its panel out beside the strip (a click elsewhere or Esc puts it away), and « brings the panels back.
  • Window menu: every panel by name, ticked while it shows. Choosing one opens it on its tab (bringing the panels back if Tab hid them, or popping it out of the icon strip), and choosing a ticked one folds it away. Then SVG Source and Icon Preview, Collapse Panels to Icons, Hide Panels (Tab), and Reset Workspace: every panel open on its first tab, the icon strip and hiding undone, SVG Source and Icon Preview docked at the standard width, and dialogs back where they first open.
  • Split view: SVG Source and Icon Preview dock in a column beside the canvas. Drag the divider at its left (or focus it and use the arrow keys) to resize it; with both open they stack, Icon Preview above SVG Source, with a divider between them. The button in each one's title bar floats it as a window of its own and docks it back. Whether each is docked, the column's width and the split are remembered. Below 1024 px wide they float.
  • Auto-Select on the Move tool's options bar: Group makes a canvas click pick the whole top-level item. Layer picks the exact shape under the cursor, even deep inside groups.
  • Rulers, guides and smart guides:
    • Rulers run along the top and left, in document pixels. Their ticks re-scale with zoom, and a marker follows the cursor. View → Rulers turns them off.
    • Guides: drag one out of a ruler. Drag it with the Move tool to reposition it (Shift rounds to 10 px), or drag it back onto a ruler to delete it. View → New Guide… places one at an exact position, and the View menu has Show Guides, Lock Guides and Clear Guides. Guides are part of undo and are saved in the file as invisible metadata (data-sc-guides).
    • Snapping: moving and drawing snap to guides, and with Smart Guides on, to the edges and centres of other objects and of the artboard. A moved selection snaps by its left, centre or right edge (and top, middle or bottom), and magenta lines show what lined up. A guide or smart match within 6 screen pixels takes priority over the grid. Hold Ctrl/⌘ while dragging to skip snapping.
  • Help: Help → SVGCraft Help (F1) opens this guide in its own tab, with every feature listed down the side and a search box. The ? on each dialog's title bar and each panel's tab bar opens the topic for it, and F1 with a dialog open goes to that dialog's topic. On a phone, Info has a Help button.
  • Status bar: an editable zoom field and the document size.
  • Theme: follows your OS by default. The sun / moon button and View → Theme switch between Dark and Light, and the choice is remembered.

Features

  • Import: Open… replaces the drawing. Import… places an SVG (as a group, scaled to fit) or a PNG / JPEG / WebP / GIF into the drawing. You can also drag and drop files, or paste SVG markup or images (Ctrl+V or Edit → Paste; Edit → Cut and Copy put the selection on the clipboard as SVG). Imported SVG (opened, imported, pasted, restored from this browser, or in a library file) is sanitised with an allowlist, because it goes into the editor's own page. Only SVG drawing elements are kept: no script, foreignObject, animation, or elements from other namespaces (such as HTML <base>, <form> or <meta>). Event handlers (on*) go. Links may only point inside the file, except image data: URLs and http(s) / mailto on <a>; they're checked as the browser reads them, so a hidden tab can't disguise javascript:. url(…) that would fetch from another server is dropped from styles and paint attributes, so opening a file never contacts anyone. <style> rules are baked into style attributes so they can't restyle the editor, and <title> / <desc> keep their text only. Root-level paint like `fill="none"

stroke="currentColor"` (common in icon sets) is pushed down so it survives.

  • Units and page size (Properties → Document). Units sets what lengths are shown and typed in: pixels, millimetres, centimetres, inches or points. That covers the rulers, W and H, guide positions, the X/Y/W/H transform fields, Image and Canvas Size, the grid (which takes a round size in the new units: 5 mm, ¼ in…) and the status bar. Strokes, type and effects stay in pixels, as in Photoshop. Page picks a size (A5, A4, A3, US Letter, Legal, Tabloid, business card, Full HD, square post) and its units, keeping the artboard's orientation; the ↻ button beside it turns the page between portrait and landscape. Inside, the drawing is always in pixels (96 per inch), so nothing changes but the numbers. A drawing in mm, cm, in or pt is saved with its real-world width and height (width="210mm"), so print, laser-cutter and plotter software know its size; the viewBox stays in pixels. Opening a file sized in real units shows it in those units; one drawn in other units (a viewBox in mm, say) is scaled to pixels, keeping its real size. Plain pixel sizes are left as they were.

Image Trace…

Turn a bitmap (a logo, icon, scan or line drawing) into vector shapes you can edit.

  1. Place the image (File → Import…, or drop it on the canvas) and select it.
  2. Choose Image → Image Trace….
  3. Pick the Preset closest to your image, then adjust the settings while you watch the preview. The line under the preview gives the result's colours, shapes and size.
  4. Click Trace. Each colour becomes its own layer in an "Image Trace" group, named like "Colour #2563eb · 34%".

Settings

  • Preset: Logo (up to 12 colours, background left out), Illustration (16), Photo (24, posterised) or Sketch (black and white). Changing a setting below switches it to Custom.
  • Colour / Greyscale / B&W: trace in colour, in greys, or in pure black and white at a Threshold you set.
  • Colours, up to: a maximum. Colours that look the same merge, so a flat logo keeps exactly the colours it has.
  • Ignore specks under: drops shapes smaller than this (noise, JPEG artefacts).
  • Smoothness: how much outlines are smoothed into curves. 0 gives pixel-exact polygons; real corners stay sharp at any setting.
  • Stacked (on by default): the largest colour goes at the bottom and each layer also covers every colour above it, so the layers overlap and no hairline gaps show. Turn it off for shapes that just touch, each only its own colour.
  • Recognise circles, ellipses and rectangles (on by default): an outline within about a pixel of one becomes a true ellipse or a rectangle (with rounded corners when they fit better). Blobs under 12 px aren't taken for boxes.
  • Ignore background: leaves out the colour round the edge of the image, where it touches the edge.
  • Keep the image (hidden): keeps the original under the trace, hidden, instead of replacing it.

Good to know

  • Best for logos, icons, illustrations, scans and line art. Photos come out posterised.
  • Each colour is taken from the solid inside of its areas, not their blended edges, so flat colours come out exact, and thin slivers of in-between colour along anti-aliased edges fold into their neighbours.
  • It reduces the image to a few colours (k-means in Lab, so similar-looking colours group together), traces each colour's outline and fits curves to it. Images are traced at 400–1000 px on the long side, in a background thread, so the page doesn't stall.
  • Image Size… (Image menu) scales the artboard and everything on it, guides included, in one undo step: width and height in pixels or percent, with Constrain proportions. It's SVG, so nothing is resampled or blurred: each top-level layer gets the scale on top of its transform, so strokes, text, patterns and gradients scale with the shapes. Scale effects (on by default, Photoshop's Scale Styles) scales layer-effect distances and sizes too (shadow, glow, blur); animation distances always follow the art.
  • Canvas Size… (Image menu) changes the artboard without scaling anything: a new width and height, or Relative to add pixels (or trim them with a minus), and an anchor that says which part stays put. The centre grows or trims every side equally; a corner or edge keeps that side fixed. Content and guides shift by whole pixels and the view follows, so nothing jumps on screen. Whatever ends up outside is kept, just not exported. (Properties → Document's W and H also resize the artboard, anchored top-left.)
  • Grayscale and black & white (Image menu), as in Photoshop, changing the colours themselves, so the saved SVG really is grey: Adjustments → Desaturate (Shift+Ctrl+U, every colour to the same-lightness grey), Black & White… (Alt+Shift+Ctrl+B, Photoshop's six hue sliders and defaults, previewed live), Threshold… (pure black and white at a level you set, previewed) and Mode → Grayscale (the brightness the eye sees). They change the selected layers, or the whole drawing with nothing selected: fills, strokes, gradient stops, patterns, symbols and markers in use, Layer Style colours and embedded images, pixel by pixel. A gradient, pattern or symbol shared with layers outside the selection gets a copy of its own first, so only the selection changes. Each is one undo step; layers locked against all edits and linked (not embedded) images are left as they are.
  • Crop (Image menu): Crop to Selection and Crop to Drawing fit the artboard tightly around the selected layers, or around everything visible, rounded out to whole pixels. The box is what's actually painted, so nothing is shaved off: stroke width and position (Center, Inside, Outside), mitre tips at sharp corners (up to the mitre limit), square and round caps, round joins, and effects (drop shadow, outer glow, blur) all count, including on rotated and scaled layers. Hidden layers don't count. Define Pattern and Copy as SVG frame the selection the same way. The drawing and the guides shift so the artboard still starts at 0, 0, and nothing moves on screen. Anything left outside the artboard is kept, but it isn't exported.
  • Select menu: All (Ctrl+A), Deselect (Esc) and Inverse (Shift+F7, or Ctrl+Shift+I where the browser allows it), which selects every visible layer that wasn't selected. If the selection includes a shape inside a group, Inverse works with individual shapes. Otherwise it works with top-level layers.
  • History panel (Window → History), as in Photoshop: every step since the drawing was opened, named by what made it (the menu command or shortcut, the tool you dragged with, the panel control you changed). Click a step to go back to it; the steps after it dim, and come back with redo until a new change replaces them.
  • Documents: every open drawing gets a tab, as in Photoshop.
    • File → New… (or + in the tab bar) opens Photoshop's New Document dialog. Pick a preset from Recent (the last five sizes you made), Web, Social (Instagram, stories, X, link previews, YouTube, LinkedIn), Mobile (iPhone, Android, iPad, Apple Watch) or Print (A5–A2, US Letter, Legal, Tabloid, business card, postcard, poster), or type a width and height in any units. Then set the name, orientation and Background: Transparent, or a White, Black or custom colour, which becomes a "Background" layer at the bottom, locked in place as in Photoshop (recolour it, or unlock and delete it). Create, Enter or double-clicking a preset makes the tab. The dialog remembers your last settings; Icon templates… switches to New Icon. Open puts a file in a tab of its own, reusing an untouched Untitled tab. Close (the tab's ✕, a middle-click, or File → Close) asks first if the drawing has unsaved changes. Closing the last tab leaves a blank workspace, as in Photoshop: only New, Open (or dropping a file on it) and the view settings work until a drawing is open, and it stays blank after a reload.
    • Each tab keeps its own drawing, undo history and zoom.
    • A drawing opens fitted to the window, and stays fitted while the canvas changes size (a pane docking, panels folding, the window resized, a phone turned) until you zoom or pan it yourself. A fitted drawing comes back fitted, whatever size the window is then.
    • A * after the name means the drawing differs from the version last opened or saved. Save (Ctrl+S) clears the *, as does the Export download. Undoing back to the saved version clears it too. PNG export doesn't count as saving.
    • Save (Ctrl+S) and Save As… (Ctrl+Shift+S), as in Photoshop. In Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers, a drawing opened from a file (File → Open, dropped on the window, or opened with the installed app) saves straight back to that file; the browser asks once a session before letting the page change it. A new drawing asks where to save the first time, and Save As… saves to a new file and carries on there. The link to the file is kept with the drawing in this browser, so Save still goes back to it after a reload. Browsers that can't write to files (Firefox, Safari, phones) download the SVG instead, and the menu says Download SVG.
    • All open drawings are kept in this browser (IndexedDB) as they change, so a reload or a later visit brings back the same tabs, the same * marks and the same view. Saving waits for a pause in your changes, but closing or reloading the page saves at once, so even the last change survives. The browser's copy is per browser and per machine; Save to keep a file. A drawing autosaved by an older version of SVGCraft is brought over as a tab.
  • Export: SVG download (the Export button), PNG at 1× / 2× / 4× with a transparent background, and Copy, which puts the drawing (or the selection) on the clipboard as SVG markup.
  • Export Clean SVG… (File menu) saves <name>.min.svg: plain SVG for the web or another app. It draws exactly the same (effects, clips, masks, gradients and patterns stay as the real SVG that draws them), but leaves out what SVGCraft keeps to reopen the file editable: every data-* attribute (layer names, locks, effect settings, guides…), unreferenced ids, unused defs, comments, empty and attribute-free groups and attributes set to their defaults. Options, remembered:
    • Decimal places for coordinates (2 by default; path data is compacted too).
    • Minify: one line, with short ids.
    • Scale to fit: only a viewBox, no width and height.
    • Leave out hidden layers.
    • Keep File Info: the title, description and licence.
    • Solid colours as currentColor, for one-colour icons a page can recolour with CSS.

    Keep Save for your working copy: a clean SVG reopens as plain shapes.

  • Shape tools (U), Photoshop's group: Rectangle, Ellipse, Triangle, Polygon (sides, and a Star ratio below 100% pulls every other point in), Line (with Arrowheads at the start, end or both) and Custom Shape (any shape from the Symbols library, drawn into the box you drag with its proportions kept). The toolbar shows one Shape button, the last tool used; hold it, right-click it or Alt-click it for the flyout, and Shift+U steps through the group (R, O and L still pick the rectangle, ellipse and line). Drag a box: Shift makes the sides equal, Alt draws from the centre. Click without dragging for Photoshop's Create box: an exact width and height (in the document's units), plus the corner radius, sides or star ratio, from the corner or the centre. A polygon or star stays live: Properties changes its sides and star ratio later, until you edit its points by hand. Arrowheads are one shared SVG marker drawn in each line's own stroke colour (context-stroke), sized by its stroke width; Properties turns them on or off for any selected line or open path.
  • Pencil: freehand drawing with adjustable smoothing (RDP simplification plus a Catmull-Rom → Bézier fit).
  • Pen: click for corners, drag for smooth curves, click the first point to close. Enter or double-click finishes, Backspace removes the last point, and Shift snaps to 45°.
  • Free Transform and Edit → Transform, as in Photoshop:
    • Free Transform (Alt+T) opens a transform session. Drag corners to scale and the top knob to rotate, or type exact X, Y, W, H (with a proportion lock), an angle, and horizontal or vertical skew into the options bar. Enter or ✓ commits. Esc or ✕ cancels the whole session.
    • Transform → Scale / Rotate / Skew open the same session with the handles set to that job: corners and edges only scale, any handle rotates, or edge handles slide along their edge to skew. Shift snaps angles to 15°.
    • Rotate 180°, Rotate 90° Clockwise / Counter Clockwise, Flip Horizontal / Vertical each apply in one step, about the selection's centre.
    • Again (Alt+Shift+T) repeats the last transform about the selection's current centre. Again with Copy (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T) duplicates first, so a 30° rotation repeated 11 times makes a ring of 12.
    • Browsers reserve Ctrl+T and Ctrl+Shift+T for tabs, so these shortcuts use Alt. Distort, Perspective and Warp aren't included, because SVG transforms can only express straight-line (affine) changes.
  • Align / distribute: from the Move tool's options bar or Layer → Align / Distribute. Align left, centre or right edges, or top, middle or bottom, to the selection's bounds. With one object selected, it aligns to the artboard instead, as in Photoshop. Distribute spaces three or more objects with equal gaps and leaves the outermost two where they are.
  • Eyedropper (I): Style mode copies a shape's fill, stroke, alpha, stroke width and opacity into the current settings, and applies them to anything selected. Colour mode samples the exact rendered pixel, including blended transparency and placed images, into the active paint. A ring around the cursor previews the colour, and Alt-click sends it to the other paint. In Chromium browsers, the eyedropper button on the Color panel can pick a colour from anywhere on screen.
  • Edit points (A, or double-click a shape): drag points and Bézier handles, Shift-click or drag round them to pick several (a rectangle, an oval or a freeform lasso, picked like the Shape tools from the Edit Points button's flyout, or with Shift+A; as in Photoshop, a drag begun with Shift adds to what's picked and one begun with Alt takes points away, and Alt pressed during a drag grows a rectangle or oval from its centre), and nudge with the arrow keys. Double-click a segment to add a point, or a point to switch it between corner and smooth. Delete removes points, and Close / open toggles the closing segment. Smooth points keep their handles in line; Alt-drag a handle to break one. Works on paths with any command (arcs included) and on rectangles, ellipses, circles, lines, polylines and polygons. A basic shape turns into a <path> only once you change it.
  • Fill rule and path direction (Properties, when a path, polygon or polyline is selected; also Object → Path). Where a path crosses itself or holds another subpath, the fill rule decides what's inside: Non-zero (SVG's default) fills an area unless the outline's directions around it cancel out; Even-odd makes every nested loop a hole, whichever way it runs. It's set on each selected shape, inside groups too, and saved as fill-rule (nothing for non-zero, unless a group or style above would make it even-odd). Reverse (Reverse Path Direction) runs the selected paths, polygons, polylines and lines the other way: under non-zero, a loop running against its outer shape is a hole; it also flips where text on the path starts and which way dashes and markers run. A closed path keeps its starting point. Rectangles, circles and ellipses become paths (a live rectangle's corners stop being editable as corners).
  • Animate (the Animation tab, when one layer or group is selected). Add animations from presets: entrances (Fade, Slide, Pop and Zoom in), exits (Fade, Slide and Zoom out), loops (Spin, Pulse, Bounce, Shake, Float, Blink), line effects (Draw on, Draw off, Dash march) and Colour cycle. Each has a length, delay, number of times or forever, direction (normal, reverse, back and forth) and easing, plus its own options (slide side and distance, turns, how far to grow, the colour to cycle to). A layer can have several, which play together, each after its own delay. Start after the one above chains one to the end of the previous (after its first run, if that one loops forever), with its delay counted from there, so an entrance, a loop and an exit can follow one another without adding up delays. Drag a row's ⠿ grip, or press Alt+↑ / Alt+↓, to reorder them; when two move or scale the layer, they combine in list order. ▶ Play (or View → Play Animations) previews the whole drawing, and Esc, a click on the canvas or any edit stops it. They're kept as settings on the layer (data-sc-anim) and written out as SVG animation (SMIL: <animate>, <animateTransform>, <set>) only when the drawing is saved, so editing and undo always see the shapes at rest. Moves, spins and scales are additive, so they happen about the layer's own centre, on top of its transform. SMIL plays in every current browser, including SVG shown in an <img> tag. Each animation adds about 150–300 bytes; Export Clean SVG keeps the animation and rounds its coordinates like the rest. PNG, app icon and favicon exports use the still drawing. Reopening a saved file rebuilds the animations from their settings.
  • Zoom (Z), as in Photoshop: click to zoom in one step (50%, 66.7%, 100%, 200%, 300% …), and Alt-click or the options bar's Zoom Out button to step out. With Scrubby Zoom on, drag right to zoom in and left to zoom out, centred where you pressed. With it off, drag a box to fill the window with that area. 100%, Fit Screen and Fill Screen are in the options bar, and double-clicking the tool goes to 100%.
  • The page itself doesn't zoom. The browser's zoom keys (Ctrl/⌘ + =, − and 0) zoom the canvas instead, like Photoshop's, and Ctrl/⌘ + wheel or a pinch only zooms the canvas, never the panels. On phones and tablets the page can't be pinched or double-tapped bigger.
  • Pixel grid and Snap to Pixel (View menu, or the checkboxes under Document in Properties): the pixel grid is a 1 px grid over the artboard from 600% zoom up. Snap to Pixel puts points and moved shapes on whole pixels, so edges stay sharp in PNG exports and at small sizes. A centred stroke of odd whole width (1, 3 px …) snaps to half pixels instead, so its edges land on whole pixels. Guides and smart guides still win when they're close, and Snap to Grid wins when it's on. Both are remembered.
  • Eraser: Object mode deletes anything you rub. Cut mode splits stroked lines and paths where you rub and leaves filled shapes alone.
  • Gradients, for fill and stroke:
    • Set a paint's Type to Solid, Linear or Radial in the Color panel.
    • Gradient editor: click the bar to add a stop, drag a stop to move it, or drag it down off the bar to remove it. Each stop has a colour, opacity and location. There's also an angle field, Reverse, a Presets list (Colour → Transparent plus everything in the Gradients panel) and a + button that saves the gradient to the Gradients panel. With a gradient active, clicking a swatch recolours the selected stop.
    • Gradient tool (G): drag across the selection to lay the gradient (Shift snaps to 45°). Radial drags from the centre outwards. Drag the end handles on the canvas to adjust it.
    • Each shape gets its own gradient in its own coordinates, so angles stay true and the gradient moves, rotates and scales with the shape. Duplicates split off their own copy when edited, unused gradients are removed automatically, and gradients in imported files are read, including ones that borrow stops from another gradient.
  • Stroke options, in the options bar of the drawing tools and under Stroke in the Color panel, so they show whatever other panel is open:
    • Width (thickness) in px.
    • Align: Inside, Center or Outside, as in Photoshop, for closed shapes (rectangles, ellipses, polygons and closed paths). SVG strokes are always centred, so an aligned stroke is drawn twice as wide and the unwanted half is hidden: clipped to the shape for Inside, and painted under the fill for Outside (masked when there's no fill). The width you set stays the visible width. Under a semi-transparent fill, the hidden half of an Outside stroke shows through faintly. Opening a path puts its stroke back to Center.
    • Caps: butt, round or square line ends.
    • Joins: miter, round or bevel corners.
    • Dashes: solid, dashed, dotted or long dash. Dash lengths are sized in multiples of the stroke width, as in Photoshop, so they keep their proportions when the width changes. They also allow for round and square caps, which extend each dash, so dotted lines come out as round dots. Custom opens Photoshop's dash / gap fields under them: up to three dash-and-gap pairs, in stroke widths. Imported dash patterns show up there too.
  • Rounded rectangles:
    • Set a Radius on the Rectangle tool's options bar before drawing, or edit a selected rectangle's four corners in Properties. The link toggle changes them all together.
    • Or drag the round handles inside the corners on the canvas. Alt-drag moves a single corner, as in Photoshop's live corners.
    • Equal corners stay a plain <rect rx>. Unequal corners become a path that remembers it's a rectangle, so its radii stay editable until you edit its points.
  • Patterns, for fill and stroke:
    • Set a paint's Type to Pattern, or click a tile in the Patterns panel. The built-ins (stripes, diagonal, dots, grid, checks, crosshatch, waves, bricks, triangles) are drawn in the paint's colour, so changing the colour re-inks them.
    • The pattern editor in the Color panel sets Scale and Angle and picks another pattern. The tiles start at the shape's top-left corner.
    • Edit → Define Pattern… turns the selection into a pattern tile the size of its visible box, as in Photoshop. It looks the same as it does on the canvas, including transforms, gradients and clip paths.
    • As with gradients, each shape gets its own <pattern> in its own coordinates, so the pattern moves and rotates with the shape. Patterns export as plain SVG.
  • Libraries: the Swatches, Gradients and Patterns panels are saved in this browser (localStorage), like Photoshop's presets.
    • + adds the current colour (with its alpha), saves the active gradient, or defines a pattern from the selection. Each asks for a name.
    • Click a tile to apply it to the active paint, or Shift-click to apply it to the other one. Double-click renames it, Alt-click deletes it, and the bar's buttons do the same for the selected tile. Reset brings back the built-in set for that panel.
    • Export (on any of the panels) saves the whole library, symbols included, as one svgcraft-library.zip:
      • svgcraft-library.json: everything, for SVGCraft.
      • swatches.gpl: a palette for GIMP, Inkscape and Krita.
      • swatches.css and gradients.css: CSS custom properties (--name: #hex, --name: linear-gradient(…)).
      • gradients.svg and patterns.svg: <linearGradient>, <radialGradient> and <pattern> defs for Inkscape, Illustrator and browsers, each drawn as a labelled sample. Pattern tiles draw in currentColor, set on each <pattern>.
      • symbols.svg: an SVG sprite, one <symbol id="…"> per symbol with its credit, for <use href="symbols.svg#id"/>.
      • README.txt: what each file is. Kinds with nothing in them are left out.
    • Import adds a file's contents, skipping anything you already have (the same colour, gradient, tile or symbol, whatever its name). If something new has the name of one of yours, SVGCraft asks once for the whole import: Keep both (the default; the imported one becomes "Sky 2"), Replace mine (yours keeps its name and place and takes the new definition) or Skip them. It reads the exported zip (from its svgcraft-library.json), a zip of palettes, gradients and SVGs without one (deflated or not, in folders or not), a JSON library, a GIMP palette (including GIMP 3's alpha), a GIMP gradient (.ggr), or any SVG, taking its gradients (shared stops included), patterns and symbols. Symbols from an SVG go in a category named after the file.
    • Browser storage belongs to one browser on one machine and is lost if you clear the site's data, so export to keep a copy. Pattern tiles and symbols from a file are sanitised like imported drawings.
  • Colours: fill and stroke, each with an on/off switch, a colour picker, a hex field and the Swatches panel. Press X to swap fill and stroke. Shift-click a swatch to apply it to the other target.
  • Transparency: fill alpha, stroke alpha and object opacity are separate sliders, and a checkerboard artboard shows the result.
  • Also included: rectangle, ellipse, line and text tools; select / marquee / move; resize and rotate handles (Shift keeps the ratio, Alt scales from the centre); flip; group / ungroup; z-order; duplicate; a layers list with show / hide; grid and snap; document size; zoom / pan (wheel, Ctrl+wheel, pinch, Space-drag); and undo / redo.

Type

The Type tool (T) works like Photoshop's:

  • Point and paragraph text. Click to start point text, which grows as you type. Drag a box to start paragraph text, which wraps inside the box. Enter starts a new line. Ctrl/⌘+Enter, or clicking away, finishes; Esc cancels.
  • Editing in place. Click text with the Type tool, or double-click it with Move, to edit it right on the canvas, in its own font, size, colour and rotation.
  • Fonts. The font picker (searchable, each name shown in its own face) opens on Popular: web-safe system fonts and about 40 popular Google Fonts. The whole Google Fonts catalogue, about 1,900 families, is a search away, or browse it by category (Sans, Serif, Display, Script, Mono). A search ranks names that start with what you typed first, then names with a word that does; long lists show their first 150 and narrow as you type. Each name loads a tiny preview of itself as it scrolls into view. A drawing opened from elsewhere in any Google family loads that family. In Chromium browsers, "Show fonts installed on this computer" adds your own fonts through the browser's Local Font Access permission. The Style menu only offers the weights and italics the font really has. The catalogue (google-fonts.js, 13 KB compressed) is regenerated with scripts/gen-google-fonts.mjs.
  • Options bar. Family, style, size and alignment, plus a button that opens the Character and Paragraph panels.
  • Per-character styling. While editing, select characters (drag, double-click a word, or Shift+arrows) and change the font, style, size, tracking, baseline shift, caps, super/subscript, underline, strikethrough or Fill colour. Only those characters change. The options bar, Character panel, font picker and colour controls all keep the edit open, and they show the settings of the characters under the caret. With nothing selected, a change applies to the whole layer. Applying a setting to a selected layer when you're not editing styles the whole layer and clears that setting from its characters, as in Photoshop. Auto leading is 120% of the largest size on each line, and paragraph text wraps by the real width of every run.
  • Character panel. Size, leading (empty means Auto, 120%), tracking in thousandths of an em as in Photoshop, and baseline shift. Toggles for All Caps, Small Caps, Superscript, Subscript, Underline and Strikethrough. Colour comes from the Fill paint.
  • Paragraph panel. Alignment, paragraph box width, and Convert to Point / Paragraph Text.
  • Fonts go with your file. An exported SVG links the Google Fonts it uses, so it renders the same in any browser. A PNG export downloads those fonts and embeds them in the image, because an SVG drawn into an image isn't allowed to fetch fonts. Installed (local) fonts only look right on computers that have them.
  • Plain SVG underneath. A text layer is ordinary SVG text, one <tspan> per line and a nested <tspan> per styled run, with the settings in standard attributes. The type details survive export and import, and other editors can read the file.
  • Create Outlines. Type → Create Outlines turns text into shapes (see below).
  • Limits. No Warp Text yet. Undo while typing covers the typing itself; character-style changes are undone as part of the finished edit.

Text on a path

Illustrator's Type on a Path. Select one text layer and one path or shape (path, rectangle, ellipse, circle, polygon, polyline or line; Shift-click both), then choose Type → Text on Path, or Put Text on Path in the Properties panel.

  • One line along the path. The text's lines are joined into one, with a space where each line break was. Its fonts, per-character styles, fill, effects, blend mode, lock and name stay. The path layer stays where it is and keeps its own paint, so give it no stroke, or hide it, if you only want the text.
  • Live. Move, rotate, scale or point-edit the path layer, or the group it's in, and the text re-flows along it straight away. The text follows the path, so moving the text layer on its own leaves it on the path.
  • Options. With a text-on-path layer selected, the Properties panel shows Start (where the text starts along the path, in percent), Align (text starts at, is centred on, or ends at that point; picking one also sets Start to 0, 50 or 100%) and Flip, which puts the text on the other side of the path, running the other way. On a closed shape the text starts where the shape does: an ellipse's or circle's right-hand point, a rectangle's top-left corner.
  • Editing. Double-click the text with Move, or click it with the Type tool, to change the words. It's edited as one straight line where it starts on the path; Enter or clicking away finishes. Character panel and options-bar changes (font, size, tracking, colour, caps…) apply to the whole text and keep it on the path. Paragraph settings that need lines (box width, Convert to Paragraph Text) don't apply.
  • Release. Type → Release Text on Path (or the Properties button) turns it back into one line of point text, placed where it started on the path.
  • If the path layer is deleted, the text keeps the last shape it ran along and stays where it was, so nothing jumps or disappears. Release it to make it ordinary text again.
  • In the file. The text is a standard <text> with a <textPath> pointing at a copy of the path's shape in <defs> (SVG ignores the referenced path's own transform, so the copy is kept in the text's coordinates), plus data-sc-textpath naming the path layer's id. The path layer gets an id if it had none. The link survives Save → reopen, Import and paste (ids that clash are renamed and the link follows), undo and Duplicate: duplicating the text with its path links the copy to the copied path.

Layers

The Layers panel works like Photoshop's:

  • One row per layer. Every shape is a layer, including the shapes inside a group. Groups show as folders you can expand or collapse, and each level is indented. An imported SVG arrives as a folder named after the file, with one layer per shape inside it. Every row has a preview, groups (of what's in them) and hidden layers too; previews are drawn just after the list, the rows in view first and the rest while the browser is idle, so a long list appears at once.
  • Selecting: click a row to select it, Ctrl/⌘-click to add or remove it, and Shift-click to select a run of rows. A group and a layer inside it are never selected together.
  • Grouping: Ctrl+G, or the folder button at the bottom of the panel, puts the selected layers in a new group (Group 1, Group 2 …) where the frontmost one was. With nothing selected, it adds an empty group. Layer → Ungroup Layers dissolves a group again.
  • Merge Down (Ctrl+E) and Merge Visible (Ctrl+Shift+E), Layer menu: as in Photoshop, but the result stays vector and nothing on screen changes. Ctrl+E merges the selected layer into the one below (keeping the lower one's name), or the selected layers into one (Merge Layers), or a selected group's contents into one (Merge Group); the menu names which. Merge Visible merges every visible layer and leaves hidden ones alone. Shapes alike in every way that shows become one path (side by side, their outlines joined; overlapping, united, which looks the same only for opaque fills with no stroke); anything else becomes one group.
  • Group by Colour (Layer menu) tidies a drawing, an imported one say, into one group per colour, named after the colour or its swatch (by stroke for shapes with no fill; gradients and patterns by which one). It asks first, as it takes every group in the drawing apart and reorders the layers. The drawing looks the same afterwards: a layer only joins its colour's group when nothing of another colour that overlaps it is stacked in between, otherwise its colour gets a second group ("Red 2"). Groups whose look depends on being a group (a clipping mask, layer style, filter, blend mode, opacity below 100%, an animation) and locked ones stay whole and are grouped as one layer ("Mixed" if they hold more than one colour). One undo puts everything back.
  • Layer via Copy / Cut (Layer → New, Ctrl+J / Alt+Shift+J), as in Photoshop, put the selected part of a layer on a new layer above it. With layers selected, Layer via Copy copies them in place (Duplicate Layer offsets its copy by 10 px so it shows) and Layer via Cut lifts shapes picked inside a group (Auto-Select: Layer) out onto layers of their own, just above the group and looking the same. With points picked in Edit Points, the segments between them go to a new path drawn like the original: Copy leaves the original whole, Cut takes them out and the original splits where they were. The new layer is selected with the Move tool.
  • Reordering: drag a row. Dropping on the top half of a row puts the layer in front of it, and the bottom half puts it behind. The middle of a folder drops it inside, and the empty space at the bottom of the list sends it to the back. Dragging a selected row moves the whole selection. Layers never move on screen when they change groups, and paint they inherited from their old group (such as an icon's fill="none") goes with them.
  • Copying and deleting by drag: as in Photoshop, drop rows on the New button (the plus square) at the bottom of the panel to copy them in place, just above themselves, or on the bin to delete them. Clicking New duplicates the selection, a little offset.
  • Showing just one layer: Alt-click its eye, as in Photoshop: every other layer hides (the groups it's in stay shown). Alt-click it again and the others come back as they were.
  • Layer Style by double-click: double-click a row anywhere but its name (the thumbnail, or the space after the name).
  • Renaming: double-click a name and type. Enter saves, Esc cancels, and an empty name goes back to the automatic one. Names are saved as data-name, which Illustrator uses too, and Inkscape layer labels are read on import.
  • Blend mode and Opacity at the top of the panel, as in Photoshop: Normal, Darken, Multiply, Color Burn, Lighten, Screen, Color Dodge, Overlay, Soft Light, Hard Light, Difference, Exclusion, Hue, Saturation, Color and Luminosity, plus Pass Through for groups. Blend mode and opacity belong to a layer, and a group is a layer: on a group they apply to the group as a whole. As in Photoshop, a group starts out on Pass Through, so its layers blend with whatever is below the group. Setting the group to Normal isolates it, so its layers blend only with each other; any other mode isolates it too. They're saved as the layer's CSS (mix-blend-mode, isolation), which browsers apply to exported SVGs too.
  • Lock: Lock position stops the layer moving, scaling, rotating, flipping, nudging and aligning. Lock all stops every change: paint, styles, blend mode, point and text edits, deleting and erasing. Locked layers can still be selected, and a lock on a group covers everything in it. A padlock on the row shows the lock; click it to unlock. The same commands are in Layer → Lock Position / Lock All / Unlock.
  • Layer Style (fx): the fx button at the bottom of the panel, Layer → Layer Style…, or double-clicking a layer's fx badge opens Photoshop's Layer Style dialog. Effects are listed down the left: tick one to turn it on, or click its name to turn it on and edit it. The canvas previews the changes as you edit (untick Preview to compare). OK keeps them, and Cancel or Esc puts everything back.
    • Drop Shadow and Inner Shadow: colour, opacity, angle, distance, spread / choke and size.
    • Outer Glow and Inner Glow: colour, opacity, spread / choke and size.
    • Color Overlay: colour and opacity.
    • Gaussian Blur: radius.
    • Blending Options: blend mode and opacity.
    • Angles, distances and sizes are in document pixels, as in Photoshop, so a rotated or scaled layer still casts its shadow the same way. Each layer gets its own SVG <filter>, which follows the layer as it changes and is exported with it. Layer → Clear Layer Style removes the effects.
  • Everything works at any depth. Move, scale, rotate, flip, nudge, align, distribute, duplicate, copy, colours, the eraser and point editing all work on a layer inside a group, so you never have to ungroup first.

Tooltips

Hover over any button for a tooltip. Tools also show a one-line description of what they do. Tooltips float above everything, panels and menus included, and fade after three seconds. Tabbing to a button shows its tip too, and on a touch screen a tap shows it briefly.

Combine Shapes

Object → Combine Shapes, or the four buttons in the Move tool's options bar, merges the selected shapes into one path, as Photoshop and Illustrator do:

  • Unite: the outline of all the shapes together.
  • Subtract Front: the backmost shape minus everything in front of it.
  • Intersect: only the area where all the shapes overlap.
  • Exclude: the areas where an odd number of shapes overlap, so the overlaps become holes.

The result takes the place, name and style of the topmost shape (the backmost one for Subtract Front), and keeps its curves, so you can point-edit it straight away. A group counts as one shape made of everything in it. Rotated, scaled and nested layers combine where they are on screen. Text and images are skipped, and you get a message saying so. The geometry comes from paper.js, which loads the first time you combine shapes.

Clipping masks

Layer → Clipping Mask → Make (Ctrl+Alt+G), or the scissors button at the bottom of the Layers panel, clips the selected layers to the topmost of them, as Illustrator does. The topmost selected layer is the clipping path, and it has to be a single shape or a text layer; anything else (a group, an image) gets a message saying why, and nothing changes. Everything selected goes into a new "Clipping group" where the clipping path was, without moving on screen. Only the art inside the clipping path's outline shows; the clipping path itself isn't painted.

The clipping path stays in the group as an ordinary layer, so the clip stays live. In the Layers panel the group and the clipping path are marked with scissors, and the clipping path's name is underlined. Click its row to select it, then move, transform or point-edit it: the window changes and the art stays put. Moving the whole group moves both together. Drop another layer into the group to clip it too. Deleting the clipping path, or dragging it out of the group, ends the clip.

Layer → Clipping Mask → Release (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+G), with the group or any layer in it selected, turns the clip off: the clipping path shows again with its own fill and stroke, and the layers stay grouped. Duplicated clipping groups clip on their own. Locked layers can't be clipped, and a locked clipping group can't be released. The clip is saved in the file and is still live when you open it again.

Create Outlines

Type → Create Outlines (Ctrl+Shift+O), Illustrator's Create Outlines and Photoshop's Convert to Shape, turns the selected text layers (or the text inside selected groups) into filled paths that look exactly like the text did, so the drawing no longer needs the fonts and the letters can be point-edited:

  • Placed as drawn. Every character goes where the browser drew it, so kerning, tracking, alignment, line spacing, paragraph wrapping, baseline shift, super/subscript and rotation all carry over. All Caps becomes capitals and Small Caps becomes smaller capitals.
  • One path per style. Each layer becomes a group named "… (outlines)" holding one path per character style, in that style's fill, stroke and opacity, so a bold word or a red word is its own path. Underline and strikethrough become bars in the same paths.
  • Keeps the layer. The group takes the text's place in the stack, its transform, Layer Style effects, blend mode, opacity, lock and hidden state. One undo brings the text back.
  • Fonts. The glyph shapes come from the real font files. Google Fonts download from Fontsource's CDN (jsDelivr), with extra character sets (Latin Extended, Cyrillic, Greek, Vietnamese) fetched only when the text needs them. Fonts installed on your computer are read directly once you've allowed installed fonts in the font picker (Chromium only). Otherwise system fonts use open stand-ins, and the message says which: Arimo for Arial and Helvetica, Tinos for Times New Roman, Cousine for Courier New (these three match the originals letter for letter), Gelasio for Georgia, DejaVu Sans for Verdana, Fira Sans for Trebuchet MS, Anton for Impact and Roboto for System UI. A font the browser fakes (an italic the family doesn't have) is slanted the same way.
  • If a font can't be downloaded (offline, say), that layer is left as text and the message says why.
  • Limits. Characters are outlined one by one, so ligatures and the joined forms of scripts like Arabic and Devanagari aren't reproduced, and Small Caps uses scaled capitals rather than a font's own small caps. A gradient that fills text is measured against each path rather than the whole line. A bold the family doesn't have, which the browser fakes by thickening the letters, comes out at the family's nearest real weight. The glyph shapes come from opentype.js, which loads the first time you create outlines.

Icons

Tools for drawing icons (see also the pixel grid and Snap to Pixel, under Features):

  • File → New Icon… makes a square artboard. Type a size or pick a common one (16 to 2048) from the size box's list, and a margin: the margins become ordinary guides on all four sides, plus centre guides if you like, so they move, lock, snap and save like any other guide. The margin follows the size (a twelfth of it) until you type your own. An untouched Untitled tab gives way to the icon.
  • Templates from the platforms' guidelines set the size and margins, say what the guides mean, and set the icon preview's mask:
    • Material system icon: 24 px with 2 px padding.
    • Favicon: 32 px.
    • Android adaptive launcher icon: 108 dp at 4× (432 px), with guides around the 72 dp area launchers show and the 66 dp safe zone inside it. Preview: circle mask, adaptive crop.
    • Google Play icon: 512 px, full bleed. Preview: rounded mask.
    • iOS app icon: 1024 px, full bleed (iOS rounds the corners itself). Preview: iOS mask.
    • macOS app icon: 1024 px with guides around the 824 px body.
  • View → Icon Keylines draws Material's keyline shapes in the live area: a circle, a square, upright and wide rectangles, the diagonals and centre lines. Sizing an icon's main shape to the keyline that matches it makes round, square, tall and wide icons look equally big side by side. The live area is inside the guides nearest each edge, so moving a margin guide moves the keylines (without guides it's a twelfth in from each edge). Keylines aren't part of the drawing.
  • Window → Icon Preview (Ctrl+Alt+P) shows the drawing at 16, 24, 32, 48, 64 and 128 px in a pane docked beside the canvas (see Split view): the button in its title bar floats it and docks it back. The previews are drawn by the browser just as a web page would draw the SVG. They update as you work, and clicking a size shows the canvas at that size. Its options (and whether it's docked, and how wide) are remembered:
    • Background: light, dark or transparent (checkerboard), or all three. It starts on the app's theme.
    • Mask: how platforms crop app icons: iOS (a rounded square, as iOS and macOS draw app icons), Circle and Squircle (Android launchers), Rounded (Google Play and Android, corners rounded by a fifth), or none.
    • Adaptive crop shows only the middle 72 dp of a 108 dp Android adaptive icon, the part launchers show (and mask).
  • File → Export App Icons… saves <name>-app-icons.zip with every size each platform asks for, each drawn from the vector art (not scaled from one big bitmap). Pick the platforms:
    • Web: favicon.ico (16, 32 and 48 px), favicon.svg, apple-touch-icon.png (180), icon-192.png and icon-512.png, a site.webmanifest and head.html, the <link> tags to paste into your pages.
    • iOS: AppIcon.appiconset (one 1024 px icon and its Contents.json) to drag into an Xcode asset catalogue.
    • Android: a res/ folder to copy into app/src/main/, and the 512 px Play Store icon. It has an adaptive icon (Android 8+): 108 dp foreground, background and monochrome layers for mdpi to xxxhdpi, and mipmap-anydpi-v26/ic_launcher.xml and ic_launcher_round.xml tying them together. The monochrome layer is the foreground's shape, for Android 13's themed icons. There are also legacy square and round ic_launcher PNGs (48 to 192 px) for older launchers.
      • A top-level layer named Background becomes the background layer, and the rest the foreground. Without one, the background is the Background colour (values/ic_launcher_background.xml).
      • Artwork drawn on New Icon's Android adaptive template (a 108 dp canvas, recognised by its guides 1/6 in) is used as drawn, edge to edge; the legacy and Play Store icons show its middle 72 dp, as a launcher does. Any other icon is fitted into the 66 dp safe zone, so no launcher mask cuts into it.
    • macOS: AppIcon.icns, and the AppIcon.iconset it's built from (16 to 1024 px), for iconutil.
    • The iOS icon and the Apple touch icon can't be transparent: they're filled with the Background colour (as is Android's adaptive background, when there's no Background layer) and saved without an alpha channel, as the App Store requires. The rest keep their transparency. A non-square artboard is centred in each square icon.

Symbols

A symbol is artwork you reuse: draw it once, place it as often as you like, and change every copy at once by editing the symbol. As in Illustrator:

  • Object → Make Symbol… asks for a name and turns the selection into a symbol. The selection is replaced by one _instance_ of it, exactly where it was, so nothing moves on screen. Effects, gradients and patterns the artwork uses go with it.
  • The Symbols panel (next to Properties, Character and Paragraph) shows the drawing's symbols. Click one, then Place to add an instance in the middle of the view, or double-click it, or drag it onto the canvas to drop one where you let go. Rename a symbol with the pen button or by double-clicking its name; instances still called after it follow the new name. Deleting a symbol that has instances asks whether to Break Links (the instances stay, as ordinary groups) or Delete Instances too.
  • Instances are layers like any other. Select, move, scale, rotate, flip, align, duplicate, lock, hide, set their opacity, blend mode and Layer Style. The Layers panel marks them with a clover and shows the symbol's name. A colour you give an instance goes onto the instance, so it only shows on the parts of the symbol that don't have a colour of their own; to recolour the artwork itself, edit the symbol.
  • Edit Symbol: double-click an instance (or use Object → Edit Symbol, or the panel's nib button). The rest of the drawing dims and steps back, and the symbol's artwork appears in place of that instance, ready to edit with every tool. Anything you draw goes into the symbol. Every other instance follows as you work. Click Done in the bar at the top, press Esc, or double-click an empty spot to finish. Each edit is a step in the drawing's undo history; undoing while you edit keeps you editing.
  • Object → Break Link to Symbol turns the selected instances into ordinary groups of the symbol's artwork, which no longer follow the symbol. They get their own copies of any gradients or effects inside.

Symbols are saved as real SVG <symbol> and <use> elements, so other viewers draw them too. They survive saving and reopening, importing into another drawing (where clashing ids are renamed and the instances follow) and copy and paste (pasting instances of a symbol the drawing already has reuses it). Define Pattern on an instance takes the symbol into the tile. Symbols in an imported file, including the top-level <symbol>s of icon sprite sheets, show up in the panel.

The Symbols library

The Symbols panel has two views: This drawing (the drawing's own symbols, above) and Library, symbols you keep across drawings. The library lives in this browser with the swatches, gradients and patterns, and travels in the same Export / Import Library file.

  • Find one with the category menu and the search box, which matches names and categories.
  • Place it with the clone button, by double-clicking it, or by dragging it onto the canvas. Placing adds the symbol to the drawing's own symbols (reusing it if the drawing already has the same artwork, so placing an icon ten times gives one symbol and ten instances) and puts an instance in the middle of the view, or where you drop it. From then on it's an ordinary symbol: edit it, break its link, rename it.
  • Save to Library (the book button under This drawing, or the plus button in the library) copies the drawing's selected symbol, or the selected instance's, into the library, at the size it is. Saved symbols go in the _Saved_ category.
  • Rename an entry by double-clicking its name or with the pen button, and delete it with the bin button or Alt-click. Reset puts the built-in icons back (and only touches the symbols).

The library starts with a built-in set of 80 icons from Font Awesome Free 6.7.2 in eleven categories: Arrows, Shapes, Interface, Communication, Weather, People, Objects, Nature, Charts, Faces and Places. They're placed 64 px tall and in the current fill colour. The icons don't set a colour of their own, so the instance's fill paints them: select an instance and pick a colour in the Color or Swatches panel to recolour it. Each icon's <symbol> carries its credit (data-credit="Font Awesome Free 6.7.2 — CC BY 4.0"), so the attribution stays in any drawing that uses it.

Library files are checked on the way in like any imported drawing: scripts, event handlers, javascript: links and style sheets are taken out of imported symbols, and entries that don't make sense are skipped.

File Info

File → File Info… (Alt+Shift+Ctrl+I, as in Photoshop; Inkscape calls it Document Metadata) describes the drawing: Title, Author, Description, Keywords (comma separated), Date (today's date to start with, free text), Copyright Status (Unknown, Copyrighted, Public Domain), Copyright Notice, Licence, Source / Info URL and Language. The licence is one of CC BY, BY-SA, BY-ND, BY-NC and BY-NC-SA 4.0, CC0 1.0, All rights reserved, or a custom URL. The source and a custom licence must be http:// or https:// addresses; anything else is refused with a note under the fields.

  • OK is one undo step and puts the * on the tab; Cancel or Esc throws the edits away. Each tab has its own File Info, and it comes back with the tab after a reload.
  • A titled drawing's tab shows the title in its tooltip.
  • Saved as standard SVG. The title and description become the root's first <title> and <desc> (screen readers read them, and browsers show the title as a tooltip). Everything goes into a <metadata> block of RDF/XML in the shape Inkscape writes: a cc:Work with Dublin Core dc:title, dc:creator and dc:rights (each a cc:Agent), dc:date, dc:description, dc:subject (an rdf:Bag of keywords), dc:source, dc:language and cc:license, followed by a cc:License block listing what a Creative Commons licence permits, requires and prohibits. Copyright Status uses XMP's xmpRights:Marked (True copyrighted, False public domain, left out when unknown), and All rights reserved is xmpRights:UsageTerms, as Adobe's apps do. The values are written with the DOM's XML APIs, so <, &, quotes and emoji are escaped properly.
  • Read back from files. Open reads that RDF, including files from Inkscape (older http:// Creative Commons URLs are recognised and written back as https://), and falls back to a plain <title> / <desc>. Only text and http(s) URLs are taken from it: nothing in a <metadata> block ever enters the drawing, and none of it (or Inkscape's sodipodi:namedview) shows up as a layer.
  • Import keeps your File Info. Importing or pasting an SVG into a drawing leaves the drawing's own File Info alone. Copy and cut of a selection leave the document's File Info out, since it describes the whole drawing. Copy as SVG markup with nothing selected copies the whole file, File Info included.
  • Other RDF fields Inkscape can write (publisher, contributors, identifier, relation, coverage) aren't kept; a field the dialog doesn't show is dropped when the file is saved again.

Shift+F7 Select inverse
Alt+T · Alt+Shift+T Free Transform · Transform Again
Ctrl+G · Ctrl+Shift+G Group · ungroup
Ctrl+Alt+G (+ Shift) Make / release clipping mask
Ctrl+Shift+O Create Outlines
Ctrl+] [ · Ctrl+Shift+] [ Bring forward / send backward · to front / to back
Arrows (Shift = 10) Nudge
Del / Backspace Delete
+ − 0 1 (or Ctrl + − 0) Zoom in / out · fit · 100%
Ctrl+R · Ctrl+; · Ctrl+' Rulers · guides · grid
Ctrl+Shift+; · Ctrl+Alt+; Snap to grid · lock guides
Ctrl+Alt+I · Ctrl+Alt+C Image Size · Canvas Size
Tab · Shift+Tab Hide all panels · hide the right-hand panels
Ctrl+S · Ctrl+Shift+S Save · Save As…
Ctrl+O Open
Ctrl+U Show / hide the SVG source
Ctrl+Alt+P Show / hide the icon preview
Alt+Shift+Ctrl+I File Info
Alt+↑ · Alt+↓ Move the animation up · down the list

The keys follow Photoshop's. A browser keeps a few for itself, so those differ: Free Transform is Alt+T (Ctrl+T opens a tab), Layer via Cut is Alt+Shift+J (Ctrl+Shift+J opens the console in Chrome and Firefox), Select Inverse is Shift+F7 (Ctrl+Shift+I opens the developer tools in some browsers), and New is in the File menu (Ctrl+N opens a window). On a Mac, Cmd+Opt+I may open the developer tools instead of Image Size. Tab hides the panels only while you're working on the canvas; with a control focused it moves focus as usual. Every tooltip ends with its control's shortcut in parentheses, taken from the menus, so they always agree. A shortcut for a menu item that's greyed out does nothing.

SVG source

Window → SVG Source (Ctrl+U, as in a browser's view-source) opens a split view beside the canvas (see Split view; float it with the button in its title bar) with the drawing's SVG, exactly as Save would write it, including the @import for any Google Fonts. It's read-only, and beautified as Prettier would lay it out: one element per line, indented by nesting; a tag too long for its line gets one attribute per line; and long values break where whitespace means nothing (path data at each M and between whole commands, points by pair, animation values and key lists at each ;, transforms by function, style by declaration), lined up under the opening quote. <style> CSS gets one rule per block and one declaration per line. Ids, links, text and data URIs are left as they are, so Copy and Download give the same drawing, just tidier. It's coloured for tags, attributes, values, comments and text, with CSS (in <style> and style="") coloured too: selectors, at-rules such as @import, properties and values. Floated, drag the window by its title bar and resize it from its corner.

  • Live. The source follows your edits, undo and tab switches. It waits while you're selecting text in it, and keeps its scroll position.
  • Linked to the canvas. Selecting layers highlights their lines and scrolls them into view. Clicking an element's start tag selects that layer. A run inside a text layer selects the text.
  • Copy puts the whole source on the clipboard. Download saves it as an .svg file. This doesn't count as saving the drawing, so the tab keeps its *. You can also select any part of the text and copy that.
  • Find (Ctrl+F in the window) highlights every match. Enter and Shift+Enter, or F3, step through them.
  • Wrap (on to start, remembered when you turn it off) wraps long lines instead of scrolling sideways.
  • Long embedded data: URIs (images, fonts) are shortened with an … on screen, but Copy and Download give the full text. Copying a selection with the mouse copies what you see, so use Copy for those.
  • Everything in the drawing is shown as text, never run: a text layer that says <script> shows up as &lt;script&gt;, as it is in the file.
  • Large drawings stay quick: lines are drawn as they scroll into view.
  • Esc closes the window. Keys pressed inside it don't edit the drawing, apart from undo, redo, save and open.

What the saved SVG keeps

Save writes everything you set in SVGCraft into the file itself, so opening it again, or importing it into another drawing, gives back the same editable drawing:

  • layer names, hidden layers, locks, blend modes and opacity
  • effects, stroke align, custom dashes and per-corner radii
  • clipping masks, still live and editable
  • gradients, patterns, styled text runs, text on a path, guides and the document size
  • symbols and their instances
  • File Info: title, author, description, keywords, date, copyright and licence, as <title>, <desc> and RDF <metadata>. Open brings it back; Import leaves the receiving drawing's own (see File Info)

Each setting is stored on its element, as a data-* attribute (data-sc-fx, data-sc-lock, data-name, …) or as CSS, next to real SVG (<filter>, <pattern>, <clipPath>). Other viewers ignore the attributes but still draw the file correctly. Editors keep attributes with their element, which comments wouldn't survive. An optimiser told to strip data-* attributes keeps the look but loses the editable settings.

Not saved in the file: undo history and the view (they stay with the browser's open tabs), and the Swatches / Gradients / Patterns / Symbols libraries (Export Library saves those). Placed library symbols are in the file, like any other symbol.

tests/roundtrip.spec.js checks all of this.
